title: The Normal Distribution and Standardisation
quickIdea: A bell-shaped density fixed by two numbers, the mean mu and the standard deviation sigma; converting to Z = (X - mu)/sigma turns every normal question into a question about one standard curve.
remember: Density f(x) = 1/(sigma sqrt(2 pi)) exp(-(x - mu)^2/(2 sigma^2)), positive on the whole real line; mean mu, variance sigma^2, standard deviation sigma.
Read the parameters off the exponent: if f is proportional to exp(-x^2/18) then 2 sigma^2 = 18, so sigma = 3 and the variance is 9; the coefficient 1/(3 sqrt(2 pi)) confirms it.
Standardise with Z = (X - mu)/sigma, which has mean 0 and variance 1. Then P(X <= x) = P(Z <= (x - mu)/sigma).
Symmetry about mu: P(Z <= -z) = P(Z >= z), and P(Z <= 0) = 1/2. This one fact answers most GATE normal questions without a table.
The empirical rule: about 68% of the mass lies within one sigma of the mean, 95% within two, 99.7% within three.
Mean, median and mode all equal mu, and a sum of independent normal variables is normal - the only family GATE names where both facts hold.

example.prompt: X is normal with mean 1 and variance 4. Y is normal with mean -1 and unknown variance. If P(X <= -1) = P(Y >= 2), find the standard deviation of Y.
example.work: Standardise X: P(X <= -1) = P(Z <= (-1 - 1)/2) = P(Z <= -1). Standardise Y: P(Y >= 2) = P(Z >= (2 - (-1))/sigma) = P(Z >= 3/sigma). By symmetry P(Z <= -1) = P(Z >= 1). Equating the two right-tail probabilities gives 3/sigma = 1, so sigma = 3.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2008 Q.29 is this argument, and no table is needed: the equation between two tail probabilities is solved by matching the standardised distances from the mean. GATE CSE 2026 Set 2 Q.4 asks the identification step alone, where the support and the shape of the exponent decide the family.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2008 Q.29: X is normal with mean +1 and variance 4; Y is normal with mean -1 and unknown variance. If P(X <= -1) = P(Y >= 2), the standard deviation of Y is (A) 3 (B) 2 (C) sqrt(2) (D) 1.
variations.why: P(X <= -1) = P(Z <= -1) and P(Y >= 2) = P(Z >= 3/sigma_Y). Since P(Z <= -1) = P(Z >= 1), we need 3/sigma_Y = 1, so sigma_Y = 3. Option (B) 2 is the standard deviation of X, which is the number the question supplies rather than asks for.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: X is normal with mean 0 and variance 9. Find P(X <= 3), P(|X| <= 3) and the value of c with P(X > c) = 0.5.
variations.why: Standardising gives P(Z <= 1) = 0.8413 and, by symmetry, P(-1 <= Z <= 1) = 2(0.8413) - 1 = 0.6827 - the 68% of the empirical rule. The median is the mean 0 because the density is symmetric.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: A density is 1/(3 sqrt(2 pi)) exp(-(x - 5)^2/18). What are its mean and variance, and what is P(X < 5)?
variations.why: The exponent gives 2 sigma^2 = 18, so sigma = 3 and the variance is 9; the shift 5 is the mean. The probability below the mean is one half by symmetry, whatever sigma is.

trap.what: Confusing sigma with sigma^2, or forgetting to standardise before comparing two normal variables.
trap.why: The density is written with sigma in the denominator and sigma^2 in the exponent, so both appear; and two normals with different parameters cannot be compared until both are in Z units.
trap.counterexample: For the 2008 question, using variance 4 as if it were the standard deviation of X gives P(Z <= -0.5) and a different sigma_Y. For the 2026 density, reading 18 as the variance gives sigma = sqrt(18) instead of 3.

check.question: X is normal with mean 10 and standard deviation 2. Find P(X <= 12) and P(8 <= X <= 12).
check.explanation: Standardise: (12 - 10)/2 = 1 and (8 - 10)/2 = -1. The second probability is the mass within one standard deviation of the mean, which the empirical rule gives as about 68%.
